p5c4.essay:
The word 'I' is missing from this confession. Raskolnikov has walked here to tell Sonia who killed Lizaveta, and when the minute comes he cannot build the sentence. He says 'Guess,' then 'Take a good look,' and makes her read it off his face. I think that is exact psychology and also exact design, because what Dostoevsky stages in place of a statement is a repetition. The narrator says his sensations are 'terribly like the moment when he had stood over the old woman with the axe,' and then Sonia backs away with her hand out and he sees Lizaveta in her. He is doing it again, to the one person he came to for mercy. The flash of 'bitter hatred' a moment earlier belongs here too: he hates her for a second the way one hates a door one has to go through.

Then the scene turns on a gesture. The hand that pushed against his chest takes both of his, and her first articulate words are not about the dead women at all: 'what have you done to yourself?' Every other character in the book, Raskolnikov included, has treated the murder as a problem of evidence or a problem of theory. Sonia treats it as an injury, and she locates the injury in him. He notices how odd that is ('You are a strange girl, Sonia') and two tears hang on his eyelashes. Dostoevsky counts them.

What follows is the part I find most remarkable, and it is easy to read too fast. Sonia asks why, and he gives her one reason after another, each cancelled almost as it is spoken. To plunder; except that he never opened the purse. To help his mother; 'that's not the real thing either.' To become a Napoleon. To pay for a career, a speech he recites 'as though it were a lesson.' Because the old woman was a louse. Because he sulked in a garret like a spider. Because he wanted 'to have the daring.' Because the devil led him. 'That's not it' is the refrain of the chapter. The usual reading picks one of these as the true motive and treats the rest as husks: he killed 'for myself alone,' to learn whether he was 'a louse like everybody else or a man.' I mostly agree, but I would not throw the husks away. He is not hiding the reason from her. He is finding out, aloud, that he has carried a handful of reasons for months and trusted none of them. Notice how far the grand theory he defended to Porfiry in [[p3c5]] has shrunk. There it concerned benefactors of mankind. Here it is an experiment with one subject, 'I only went to try,' and by his own logic the experiment was void before it began, since a man who has to ask whether he is a Napoleon already has his answer. He knows this. 'I went into it like a wise man, and that was just my destruction.'

Sonia's part is small in words and enormous in effect. She cannot argue with him and does not try. When he opens with the hypothetical about Luzhin and Katerina Ivanovna, which is the tavern arithmetic of [[p1c6]] dressed up for her benefit, she declines the chair he offers her: 'who has made me a judge.' When he delivers the Napoleon parable she asks him to say it 'without examples.' When he says louse she hands the word back with 'a human being' in front of it. Garnett's 'louse' is blunt and right; the insect has been crawling through his thoughts since [[p3c6]], where he first suspected he was a viler one than the woman he killed. Sonia has no counter-theory, yet nothing he says survives her hearing it.

Her remedy is the strangest thing in the chapter. She does not say go to the police. She says stand at the cross-roads, kiss the earth, tell everyone. He translates at once into his own language ('You mean Siberia, Sonia?') and refuses on political grounds: 'they' destroy men by millions and call it virtue. That may even be true, and it is beside her point. What unsettles me is how fast he recovers. Within a page of 'I murdered myself' he is saying 'perhaps after all I am a man and not a louse,' the haughty smile is back, and he is briefing her on the weakness of the police case. The confession has not converted him. It has not even comforted him: sitting beside her 'as though they had been cast up by the tempest,' he finds her love 'burdensome and painful' and is unhappier than when he came. I trust the chapter because of that. A lesser novelist would have let the telling be a relief.

So the scene ends on a hand withdrawn. She offers the cypress cross; he reaches for it, then says 'Not now.' Hold on to that. And then, of all people, Lebeziatnikov knocks.

annotations.quote: who has made me a judge to decide who is to live and who is not to live?
annotations.note: He has spent the whole novel assuming this question has an answer and that a clever man can work it out. Sonia does not answer it; she refuses the seat. The phrasing has a Gospel ring (Luke 12:14, 'who made me a judge'), which in her would be instinct and not quotation.

annotations.quote: there was love in them; his hatred vanished like a phantom
annotations.note: A flash of hatred for the person he is about to need most. The narrator explains it at once as one feeling mistaken for another, and I half believe him. It reads to me as the hatred of dependence: she is about to hold his life, and he resents the hands before he puts it in them.

annotations.quote: terribly like the moment when he had stood over the old woman with the axe in his hand
annotations.note: The same compulsion, the same sense of a minute that cannot be missed. Dostoevsky ties the confession to the murder in [[p1c7]] by its bodily feel, and that is unsettling: telling is not the opposite of the act but something that comes over him in the same way.

annotations.quote: He looked at her and all at once seemed to see in her face the face of Lizaveta.
annotations.note: In [[p1c7]] Lizaveta did not shield her face; she held her empty left hand out in front of her, like a child. Sonia now makes that gesture, and even the hand is the same. For a paragraph the two of them are murderer and victim, and the two women who read the Gospel together have one face.

annotations.quote: “What have you done--what have you done to yourself?”
annotations.note: The sentence the chapter turns on. Not 'to her' or 'to them' but 'to yourself.' Sonia's first instinct is that the murderer is the person most damaged by the murder. Watch for him reaching the same thought by his own road a few pages on.

annotations.quote: had not had Toulon nor Egypt nor the passage of Mont Blanc to begin his career with
annotations.note: The stations of Napoleon's rise: the siege of Toulon, the Egyptian campaign, the crossing of the Alps. The crossing was by the Great St Bernard pass, not Mont Blanc, so either Raskolnikov or his author is hazy on the geography. What matters is the next phrase, 'picturesque and monumental.' Part of his grievance is aesthetic: his own deed had no grandeur in it.

annotations.quote: “You had better tell me straight out... without examples,”
annotations.note: My favourite line of Sonia's. He has been thinking in examples for months (Napoleon, Mahomet, lawgivers), and she asks, timidly, for the thing itself. It is the most effective criticism his theory receives, and it comes from someone who does not know it is criticism.

annotations.quote: (Yes, sulkiness, that’s the right word for it!) I sat in my room like a spider.
annotations.note: Garnett's 'sulkiness' is a small nursery word for what produced a murder, and he insists on it. He also admits here that work was available: Razumihin offered him some in [[p2c2]] and he walked out. Then the spider. Remember Svidrigaïlov's picture of eternity in [[p4c1]], a bathhouse with spiders in the corners; the image is going around.

annotations.quote: I wanted to murder without casuistry, to murder for my own sake, for myself alone!
annotations.note: 'Casuistry' is the old word for reasoning through cases of conscience, usually with the sense of reasoning one's way out of them. He wanted to be rid of his own justifications, the mother, the benefactor of mankind, and act bare. This is the nearest he comes to a motive he does not immediately take back.

annotations.quote: Did I murder the old woman? I murdered myself, not her!
annotations.note: He means it as despair and partly as evasion; the very next sentence hands the old woman to the devil. But it also agrees, almost word for word, with what Sonia cried when she first understood. They have arrived at one sentence from opposite directions.

annotations.quote: first kiss the earth which you have defiled and then bow down to all the world
annotations.note: Not a police station: a cross-roads, the ground, and everybody. Sonia's idea of confession is public and physical, and the wrong it answers is to the earth and to people in general, not to the law. He hears only 'Siberia.' Keep her exact instructions in mind.

annotations.quote: But immediately he drew back the hand he held out for the cross.
annotations.note: She offers him cypress and keeps Lizaveta's copper for herself. A cypress cross and a copper one hung on the old woman's neck beside the chamois purse in [[p1c7]], and he threw them back on her body. I doubt the match is an accident. His hand goes out and comes back.

links.why: Lizaveta's outstretched hand and childlike terror, which he sees again in Sonia's face as he tells her.
The theory in its confident public form, argued with Porfiry; set it beside the stammered, self-cancelling version he gives Sonia.
Yesterday in this same room: the reading, the promise to tell her who killed Lizaveta, and a last paragraph worth rereading before going on.
Alone on his sofa he had already called himself a louse; here he says it to another person for the first time.

p5c5.essay:
Dostoevsky follows the most inward scene in the book with Lebeziatnikov on the pavement explaining that madness is 'a logical mistake' which a Paris professor cured by argument, though he 'made use of douches too.' It is a good joke and I think a pointed one. The belief that a person is a set of propositions which can be corrected is exactly what the previous chapter took apart, and Raskolnikov's tired reply, 'Life would be too easy if it were so,' could be addressed to his own theory as much as to this fool.

The middle of the chapter is a quiet I would not skip. He goes home for no reason, listens to hammering he cannot locate, looks at the geraniums he knows 'by heart,' and thinks, with a strange smile, that perhaps Siberia would be better. Then Dounia arrives announcing that she knows 'all, all,' meaning that Razumihin has told her about the police suspicion. Her generosity is real and it rests on nothing; she offers her whole life to a brother she is picturing wrongly. What he gives back is a character reference for Razumihin, and she is quick enough to hear that it sounds like a bequest.

And then the street. Katerina Ivanovna has always lived on one possession, the idea that she is a lady, and here she takes it out to the canal bank and tries to make it pay. The children must sing in French so that people 'will see at once' what family they come from; 'My Village' is too common; the bodice was cut wrong. I find it almost unbearable and also, in flashes, funny, which is Dostoevsky's usual and unfair method. The inkpot thrown at the general is a triumph. The two little ones running off hand in hand is the moment it breaks. Her death in Sonia's room, a room she has never once visited, is as unreconciled as her life: no priest, no rouble to spare for one, and a God who 'must forgive' or be done without. Set that beside Sonia's faith a chapter ago. The book does not rule between them here. It lets the certificate of merit lie by the pillow and asks, in the narrator's own voice, how it got there.

Then the last page takes the floor out. Svidrigaïlov, benevolent and flush with money, hands Raskolnikov his own sentences back: the louse, Luzhin going on living, Polenka going 'the same way.' We were told at the end of [[p4c4]] about the chair set by the door, so the surprise is less that he listened than how he uses what he heard: 'with an air of a sort of gay winking slyness,' as a pleasantry between friends. The confession that was meant for one hearer has had two, and the second is shaking with laughter.

annotations.quote: But as he made use of douches too, how far success was due to that treatment remains uncertain
annotations.note: Garnett's 'douches' are showers: the cold-water treatment of the nineteenth-century asylum. The sentence undoes itself beautifully. Reason cured the mad, he reports, unless it was the cold water.

annotations.quote: “Perhaps it really would be better in Siberia,” he thought suddenly.
annotations.note: A strange thought indeed, an hour after 'I am not going to them.' It comes to him in the room where the whole idea was hatched, and it comes as a wish for relief, not as repentance. Note the smile that goes with it.

annotations.quote: Brother, now I know all, _all_. Dmitri Prokofitch has explained and told me everything.
annotations.note: The italics hurt. What she knows is that the police suspect him, and she takes his horror for the indignation of an innocent man. Everything loving she says in this speech is built on that.

annotations.quote: a foretaste of an eternity “on a square yard of space.”
annotations.note: His own phrase coming back. In [[p2c6]] he thought of a condemned man who would rather stand for ever on a ledge, a square yard of space, than die at once, and took it as proof of how fiercely one wants to live. Now the ledge is simply what the life ahead of him looks like.

annotations.quote: And as it is in French, people will see at once that you are children of good family
annotations.note: Her whole theory of the world in a sentence: gentility is visible, and once seen it must be honoured. French is the proof. The crowd sees a sick woman beating frightened children.

annotations.quote: “So that’s how you live, Sonia! Never once have I been in your room.”
annotations.note: A terrible small fact. The stepmother whose taunts sent Sonia out that first evening, as Marmeladov told it in [[p1c2]], has never seen where she lives. What she says next is as near to an apology as this proud woman comes.

annotations.quote: I have no sins. God must forgive me without that. He knows how I have suffered
annotations.note: Compare the priest at Marmeladov's deathbed in [[p2c7]], where she had no patience for talk of forgiveness either. She has not softened since. I find it hard not to admire a woman who presents God with a bill.

annotations.quote: in the vale!... of Dagestan!... With lead in my breast!
annotations.note: The song is a setting of Lermontov's poem 'The Dream,' in which a man lies shot in a valley in Dagestan and dreams of home. Marmeladov sang it when they were engaged. She gets as far as 'lead in my breast' with her own chest bleeding, and the look of terror suggests she hears it.

annotations.quote: And how did “the certificate of merit” come to be on the bed beside Katerina Ivanovna?
annotations.note: The narrator asks and does not answer. This is the certificate from her school days that Marmeladov described in the tavern in [[p1c2]] and that went round the table at the dinner in [[p5c2]]. She must have carried it through the streets all afternoon.

annotations.quote: who turned white and cold, hearing his own phrases, spoken to Sonia
annotations.note: Check them against [[p5c4]]: the louse, Luzhin 'doing wicked things,' Polenka going 'the same way.' Svidrigaïlov quotes accurately and lets the quotation do the work. He never says what he heard.

links.why: Marmeladov's tavern account of his wife, her certificate of merit and the family's green shawl, all of which are out on the street with her here.
The other deathbed in this family, with the same children looking on and the same quarrel with the priest.
Svidrigaïlov's first visit, where he offered the ten thousand roubles and insisted the two of them had something in common.
Its closing paragraph explains how Raskolnikov's own phrases could come back to him at the end of this chapter.
